title: Digital content creators are becoming information intermediaries faster than support systems can provide verification, ethics, safety, and platform voice
source_unit: UNESCO, Behind the Screens in South Africa: Challenges, Opportunities, and Needs of Digital Content Creators, summarized in a UNESCO research release published 1 September 2026
geography: South Africa; nationwide survey of digital content creators with supporting interviews and UNESCO Social Media 4 Peace context

observations.period: 2026; creator information practices and public-discourse role

denominator.unit: digital content creators in a nationwide South African survey

information_sources.value: 43.8% of surveyed creators rely on mainstream news media as a primary information source, while creators also conduct their own research, draw on personal experience, and consult knowledgeable experts

creator_role.value: creators increasingly produce, interpret, and share information with online audiences, expanding their role in the information ecosystem

verification_gap.value: 36% report that they do not systematically verify information before sharing it

credibility_signal.value: 34% rely on likes and views as a key indicator of credibility

observations.method: UNESCO summary of a CABC nationwide survey of 48 creators and in-depth interviews with 11 creators; small creator sample, not a representative audience or population survey.
observations.uncertainty: The source does not establish how creator practices affect audience beliefs, elections, public-health behavior, or misinformation prevalence; percentages may be sensitive to wording, self-report, sample composition, and creator type.
observations.subgroup: Digital content creators, audiences, creators relying on mainstream news, creators using personal experience or experts, and creators whose visibility is shaped by platform metrics.
observations.counterinterpretation: Personal research and expert consultation may supplement mainstream journalism rather than weaken information quality; likes and views can be useful audience feedback even when they are not reliable truth indicators.

observations.period: 2026; creator training, standards, AI disclosure, and regulation awareness

denominator.unit: digital content creators in the South African survey

media_literacy_training.value: 10.4% of creators had received Media and Information Literacy training

journalism_background.value: 50% reported having no journalism training or background

freedom_expression_awareness.value: 64.6% reported little or no awareness of international freedom-of-expression standards

regulatory_awareness.value: 59% were unaware of regulations specifically relevant to digital content creation

ai_disclosure.value: 33% consistently disclose their use of generative AI to audiences

observations.method: UNESCO summary of the CABC creator survey and interviews; measures are self-reported and the source does not provide a platform-by-platform audit of disclosures or standards compliance.
observations.uncertainty: The source does not determine whether training causes more accurate content, whether disclosure changes audience trust, or whether regulatory awareness predicts safer or more ethical practice.
observations.subgroup: Creators with and without journalism or MIL training, creators using generative AI, audiences assessing authenticity, civil-society trainers, regulators, and platforms.
observations.counterinterpretation: Creators may use AI responsibly without consistently disclosing it, and formal journalism or regulatory knowledge is not identical to accuracy, ethics, or audience benefit.

observations.period: 2026; online harm and unequal exposure in the creator ecosystem

denominator.unit: digital content creators in the South African survey

technology_gender_based_violence.value: 75% had experienced or witnessed technology-facilitated gender-based violence

xenophobia.value: 72% had experienced or witnessed xenophobia online

identity_hate.value: 43% reported identity-based hate speech or harassment

support_gap.value: the source describes significant exposure to online harms alongside limited formal training and support mechanisms

observations.method: UNESCO summary of self-reported survey and interview evidence; the findings are descriptive and do not estimate incident prevalence among all South African creators or users.
observations.uncertainty: Experience or witnessing is not equivalent to verified incident counts, frequency, severity, or causal platform attribution; the small sample may over- or under-represent creators exposed to particular harms.
observations.subgroup: Women and gender-diverse creators, migrant and racialised creators, creators discussing identity or politics, creators with high visibility, and people experiencing online abuse.
observations.counterinterpretation: High reported exposure may reflect creators’ greater visibility and reporting awareness rather than an ecosystem-wide increase; reducing harm also requires offline legal, social, and institutional support beyond platform moderation.

observations.period: 2026; creator support, platform governance, and information-ecosystem resilience

denominator.unit: digital content creators in the South African survey, with UNESCO programme support context

ethics_interest.value: 87% expressed interest in training on ethics and freedom of expression, and 87.5% saw value in ethical guidelines or standards

requested_support.value: creators identified practical workshops, peer learning, platform and AI literacy, and accessible legal and regulatory information as needed support

governance_route.value: the recommendations include creator participation in platform-governance discussions, stronger support for online harms and wellbeing, and creator-focused MIL programmes

capacity_building.value: UNESCO reports capacity-building support for 30 South African creators and MIL training for journalists, civil society, and youth organisations

observations.method: UNESCO research release combining survey findings, interviews, recommendations, and programme context; it reports activity and stated demand, not programme impact.
observations.uncertainty: The source does not establish whether training, peer networks, platform participation, or support mechanisms improve accuracy, safety, income, wellbeing, audience trust, or resilience over time.
observations.subgroup: Creators, platform firms, AI providers, media-literacy organisations, civil society, youth groups, journalists, regulators, and audiences.
observations.counterinterpretation: Creator-focused training may individualise responsibility for harms created by platform incentives, commercial partnerships, moderation systems, and unequal power; participation in governance is meaningful only if creators can influence decisions.

related_sources.claim: Official UNESCO report Behind the Screens in South Africa: Challenges, Opportunities, and Needs of Digital Content Creators.
UNESCO Social Media 4 Peace context for media and information literacy, online harms, and peacebuilding.

boundary: This record adds a creator-legitimacy and information-infrastructure subtheme: digital creators are increasingly intermediaries between audiences and information, while verification, ethics, AI disclosure, legal literacy, safety, and platform voice lag behind their influence. The evidence is a small self-reported survey of 48 creators, 11 interviews, and programme reporting; it is not representative audience evidence, a causal misinformation study, a platform audit, a creator-income study, or proof that training changes outcomes.
